stories.headline: WARSH'S HAWKISH JACKSON HOLE DEBUT SENDS YIELDS UP, STOCKS DOWN
stories.body: In his first keynote as Fed Chair, Kevin Warsh said this summer's PCE and CPI readings, while better than expected, 'do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved,' pushing September rate-hike odds to nearly 60% and the 10-year yield up 5 bps to 4.72%. The S&P 500 slid 0.25% to 7,712 and the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.70% to 29,433, though all three major indexes still closed out the week higher.
stories.explain: Long-end Treasury yields move on the market's forward expectations for the fed funds rate, not the current policy rate itself, so a speech that raises the odds of a hike repriced the curve immediately, before the Fed has done anything. Jackson Hole carries outsized weight because it is historically where chairs pre-signal policy shifts, so today's move reflects traders repositioning for tighter policy into September rather than reacting to a single data point.

stories.headline: GOLD SUFFERS WORST SESSION IN MONTHS, SLIDING AS MUCH AS 3.2% ON WARSH'S REMARKS
stories.body: Gold, which had been holding above $4,600 near a three-month high, fell as sharply as 3.2% intraday to around $4,515 before settling near $4,504, down 2.75% on the day, as Warsh's hawkish tone lifted real yields.
stories.explain: Gold pays no yield, so its cost of carry is the real (inflation-adjusted) interest rate: today's move in nominal yields outpaced any shift in inflation expectations, meaning real yields rose and made holding zero-yield gold comparatively more expensive. That single-variable sensitivity is why gold's percentage move was roughly ten times the S&P 500's on the same headline.

stories.headline: STOCKS CLOSE LOWER BUT POST A WINNING WEEK; PAYPAL SLUMPS 16%
stories.body: Despite Friday's pullback, the S&P 500 gained 0.5% on the week, the Nasdaq added 0.9%, and the Dow rose 0.5% for its first winning week in three. PayPal tumbled 16% in premarket trading after Advent and Stripe abandoned their pursuit of the company, while Elastic jumped more than 18% on strong quarterly earnings.
stories.explain: A single-day pullback inside a positive week is a reminder that daily headline moves and the underlying trend can diverge: this week's gains were built earlier on strong Nvidia-led earnings momentum, and Friday's Fed-driven dip only pared some of that advance rather than reversing it.

stories.headline: OIL FIRMS ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ TENSION EVEN AS THE DOLLAR STRENGTHENS
stories.body: WTI crude rose 0.40% to $83 a barrel as renewed concern over shipping risk through the Strait of Hormuz offset the drag of a stronger dollar, which climbed 0.51% to 99.68 on the DXY after Warsh's hawkish comments.
stories.explain: Oil is priced in dollars, so a stronger DXY is normally a headwind for crude since it makes the commodity more expensive for foreign buyers; today's gain shows a geopolitical supply-risk premium overriding that usual inverse relationship, a pattern worth watching if Strait of Hormuz tensions escalate further.

stories.headline: SEMIS SPLIT AS MARVELL AND RUBRIK FALL DESPITE BEATING ESTIMATES
stories.body: Marvell Technology and Rubrik both topped analyst expectations but saw shares decline anyway, pressuring the chip sector even as the broader market digested Warsh's remarks, a sign investors are pricing in forward guidance and rate sensitivity over the headline beat.
stories.explain: When a stock falls on a beat, it usually means the market had already priced in strong results, or guidance and margin commentary disappointed relative to those elevated expectations; that dynamic is amplified for high-multiple growth names like chipmakers, whose valuations are most sensitive to the discount-rate move a hawkish Fed speech like today's just delivered.

stories.headline: BIG 12 LANDS TWELVE FIFTH-YEAR SENIORS AS ELIGIBILITY RULINGS RESHAPE THE PORTAL
stories.body: Court decisions clearing fifth-year and formerly-professional players for eligibility have flipped the transfer portal's late-offseason economics: the Big 12 alone has added 12 fifth-year seniors in the past month, with Texas Tech, Cincinnati, BYU, West Virginia, Oklahoma State, Arizona, and Houston all landing veteran starters. Coaches are bracing for the NCAA's looming 5-in-5 eligibility model, which could close this window as fast as it opened.

stories.headline: KINGS WAIVE SIX-TIME ALL-STAR DEMAR DEROZAN; HARDEN AGREES TO RETURN TO CAVALIERS
stories.body: Sacramento waived DeMar DeRozan, instantly making the six-time All-Star one of the top names still on the open market, while James Harden agreed to a three-year, $97 million deal to rejoin Cleveland. Atlanta also added guard Lu Dort in a three-team trade with Oklahoma City and Dallas that also brought in Ryan Nembhard, part of an unusually active late-August stretch in an offseason already reshaped by Giannis Antetokounmpo's move to Miami and LeBron James's signing with Philadelphia.

stories.headline: LEAGUE RACES TO 53-MAN ROSTERS BEFORE SUNDAY'S 6 P.M. ET CUTDOWN DEADLINE
stories.body: All 32 teams are trimming from 90 to 53 players ahead of Sunday's deadline, pushed a day later than usual to accommodate the 49ers' international season-opening travel. Miami has already waived 12 players, and Cleveland's Dillon Gabriel faces an uncertain roster spot in a crowded quarterback room as clubs finalize practice squads, which can carry up to 17 players including one international slot.

stories.headline: NORTH CAROLINA UPSETS TCU 15-10 IN DUBLIN TO OPEN BILL BELICHICK'S SECOND SEASON
stories.body: North Carolina opened the 2026 FBS season with a defensive-driven 15-10 upset of TCU at Aviva Stadium in Dublin, Ireland, giving Bill Belichick a win to start Year 2 in Chapel Hill. Elsewhere on the sport's opening Saturday, No. 14 USC routed San Jose State 56-28 at the Coliseum as more than a dozen first-year Power Four coaches made their debuts.

sports.detail: No. 17 Huskies are gearing up for the Apple Cup season opener against Washington State on Sunday, Sept. 6. RB Jordan Washington took part in light warmups after a spring neck injury, though his season status remains unclear, while transfer WR Christian Moss has emerged as the likely starting X receiver and QB Demond Williams Jr. made the Maxwell Award watch list.

Rebuilding after a 16-17 finish and the departures of Hannes Steinbach (drafted 14th by Charlotte) and Zoom Diallo (transferred to Kentucky). Guard Wesley Yates III returns as the top scorer, and the Huskies added transfers from Gonzaga, San Francisco, and Texas Tech plus first 2026 signee Lattimore Ford.

The reigning Super Bowl LX champions closed the preseason with a 9-9 tie at Kansas City after Jason Myers missed a 52-yard field goal at the buzzer; third-string QB Jalen Milroe threw a touchdown in relief. Seattle opens the regular season Wednesday, Sept. 9 at home against New England — a rematch of the Super Bowl.

Contract talks with All-NBA center Jalen Duren remain contentious with training camp approaching; the restricted free agent has declined to discuss his situation publicly, and the Lakers and Kings are among the teams reportedly interested if a deal isn't reached. Open the 2026-27 season at home against Boston on Tuesday, Oct. 20.
Dropped the series opener 8-1 in Toronto on Friday and are back in action at Rogers Centre Saturday afternoon, with the series wrapping up Sunday before Seattle returns home.

deepDive.title: Why NFL Roster Cuts Are a Lesson in Sunk Cost and Dead-Cap Accounting
content: Sunday's 6 p.m. ET deadline forces all 32 NFL teams to cut from 90-man offseason rosters down to 53, a purge of roughly 1,184 players happening in real time this weekend. Miami alone has already waived a dozen players, while Cleveland faces a genuinely hard call on quarterback Dillon Gabriel in a crowded room. On the surface this looks like simple talent evaluation, but every one of those decisions is really a corporate-finance problem in miniature: teams must decide whether to keep paying a player whose guaranteed money is already committed, or eat that cost now and redirect the open roster spot toward more productive use.

The mechanism is dead-cap accounting. NFL contracts typically split pay into base salary, which is usually not guaranteed beyond the current year, and signing bonus, which is prorated evenly across the life of the deal for salary-cap purposes regardless of when it's actually paid out. If a team cuts a player, any remaining prorated bonus accelerates immediately onto that year's cap as 'dead money' — a charge for production the team will never receive — while unguaranteed base salary simply vanishes with no cap consequence. That asymmetry is exactly why the 90-to-53 cutdown is a sunk-cost exercise: the signing bonus is spent no matter what, so the only forward-looking question is whether the roster spot is worth more than the replacement available on waivers.

The extreme version of this shows why the math matters. When Denver released Russell Wilson in 2024, the Broncos absorbed roughly $85 million in dead cap — the largest single-player charge in NFL history — because so much of his contract had already been paid out as a guaranteed bonus. That case is the textbook illustration of a team correctly ignoring the sunk cost of money already spent and paying it anyway just to reclaim roster flexibility. Most of this weekend's 1,184 cuts are the opposite case: low-round or undrafted players carrying little or no guaranteed money, so the dead-cap charge is close to zero and the decision is nearly frictionless.

That is also why Cleveland's Dillon Gabriel situation is the more interesting story than Miami's dozen releases. A player with meaningful guaranteed money attached is expensive to cut even when a coaching staff has doubts, which quietly narrows a front office's real options long before Sunday's deadline arrives. The same logic will resurface at the trade deadline and in every future extension decision: the guarantee, not the talent evaluation, often decides who stays. For a finance student, NFL cutdown weekend is a clean, dollar-denominated demonstration of ignoring sunk costs and pricing only the marginal decision in front of you.
